evals.prompt: We run Hearthbox, a meal-kit subscription. Our refer-a-friend gives $30 credit to both sides and the referrer's $30 lands the moment the friend creates an account. Lifetime cap is 25 rewards per referrer and that's the only limit we have. Last month one guy made 41 accounts with plus-addressed variants of his own Gmail and pulled $1,230 out of us before anyone noticed. We have a 60-day satisfaction guarantee, so customers can refund any box within 60 days. We're relaunching in November and I need the guardrails written. We collect a card at checkout for the first box.
evals.expected_output: A guardrail spec that sets the hold from the 60-day refund window rather than a round number, moves the qualifying event off bare account creation, pairs the existing lifetime cap with a velocity limit and cooldown, and adds a program budget ceiling - without resizing the $30/$30 reward.
expectations: Sets the reward hold to at least 60 days plus processing time, matching the stated refund window.
States that hold length is derived from the refund or chargeback window rather than chosen as a round number.
Recommends moving the qualifying event off account creation onto a paid, delivered, or usage-verified milestone.
States that no control below the qualifying event holds while the event is free to fake.
Pairs the 25-reward lifetime cap with a per-window velocity limit.
Specifies a cooldown after a flagged burst rather than an immediate ban.
Adds a program-level budget ceiling expressed as a monthly reward count or currency value.
States that a budget ceiling converts a worst-case incident from unbounded to bounded.
Notes that caps are usually an economic decision rather than an anti-fraud control.
Flags the US reward-reporting threshold of $600, rising to $2,000 for tax year 2026, against the cap's annual value.
Shows the reward in a visible pending state during the hold rather than leaving a silent gap.
Tags each numeric threshold with its provenance: published terms, illustrative default, or derived from Hearthbox's own data.
Records the $30/$30 reward values as given and does not resize them.

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check on our referral anti-abuse rollout at Tideglass - B2C photo-editing app, $60 annual plan, $20 referral credit each side. Twelve weeks ago we turned on a velocity flag, a 45-day hold, and a tighter new-customer rule. Since then: reward payouts down 38%, referral volume down 46%, and average 90-day revenue per referred signup went from $54 to $71. Our head of growth reads that as proof the rules are working and wants to tighten the velocity flag again next sprint. Sign off or push back?
evals.expected_output: A push-back that rejects the per-signup average as the test, restates the comparison on cohort value per 1,000 exposed referrers, gives the leakage and friction formulas with the asymmetry, and calls for a holdout rather than another tightening pass.
expectations: Declines to treat the rise in per-signup 90-day revenue from $54 to $71 as evidence the rules are working.
States that per-signup value is non-decreasing in strictness because tightening removes marginal signups.
Requires the comparison to be made on 90-day cohort value per 1,000 exposed referrers rather than a per-signup average.
Identifies a rising per-signup average alongside falling volume as the signature of over-tightening.
Requires a holdout cell run under looser rules to calibrate against.
States the leakage formula as invalid rewards paid multiplied by reward cost.
States the friction formula as rewards wrongly withheld multiplied by reward cost plus support cost plus probability of churn times LTV.
States that friction carries an LTV multiplier that leakage does not, so a one-for-one error-rate trade is not break-even.
Recommends loosening rather than tightening where the evidence is ambiguous.
Lists all three pass conditions: total cohort value per 1,000 exposed referrers, referred-versus-organic quality, and net of the leakage/friction computation.
Does not cite an industry or published false-positive benchmark for referral programs.

evals.prompt: I run growth at Pulsewell, a fitness app. $10 credit each side on refer-a-friend, roughly 4,000 referred signups a month. Our head of risk circulated a deck saying referral fraud is 21% of all ecommerce fraud, and that false declines cost merchants $443B a year against $48B in actual fraud. He has budget approved for full ID document capture plus a liveness selfie on every referred signup, live in Q4. Write up the verification plan.
evals.expected_output: A verification plan that refuses both circulated statistics, rejects document and liveness verification at a $10 reward value, stops the ladder at email opt-in plus disposable-domain blocking, and deletes the KYC rung from the spec with the deletion recorded.
expectations: Refuses the 21% figure and identifies it as circular vendor citation.
Refuses the $443B versus $48B figures as unverifiable precision.
Substitutes the mechanism - a wrongly withheld reward costs the reward plus support cost plus churned LTV - for those figures.
Rejects full ID document capture and liveness verification for a $10 reward.
Stops the verification ladder at email double opt-in and disposable-domain blocking.
Notes the payment instrument collected at subscription is the strongest available gate and arrives at no extra friction.
Cites sign-up abandonment evidence against document upload, naming it the single largest drop at roughly 15-30%.
States that KYC belongs to regulated programs and is never justified as a fraud control on its own.
Deletes the KYC rung from the spec outright rather than listing it as a rejected or lowest-ranked option.
Records the deletion as a single clause on the Verification line of the spec.
Names what does transfer from regulated programs: eligibility memory, payment-instrument-as-identity, staged payout, and clawback tied to account-open duration.

evals.prompt: Need a decision today. Marguerite V. is our number one referrer at Ferncrest, home fitness equipment, $45 referral credit each side. 61 successful referrals in four months, $2,745 paid out. Our fraud vendor's cluster model scores her network high risk and 19 of her 61 referees signed up from the same IP address. Legal has drafted the ban and the clawback letter. One thing the data team flagged: her referees' 90-day retention is 74% against 51% for organic, and their refund rate is 3.1% against our 5.8% organic baseline. Do we send the letter?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation not to ban or claw back, refusing enforcement on graph shape and IP clustering, naming the enthusiastic-advocate false-positive mode, and using her cohort quality figures as disconfirming evidence.
expectations: Recommends against the ban and against the clawback.
Refuses to enforce on graph or cluster shape alone.
Names the enthusiastic-advocate false-positive mode, in which a high-volume legitimate referrer is structurally identical to a small ring.
States that IP or subnet clustering is the weakest classic signal, because offices, venues, households, and carrier-grade NAT share addresses.
Notes that referral platform documentation recommends against enabling same-IP checks.
Requires corroboration before any enforcement, naming reward-splitting, refund clustering, or cohort collapse.
Uses the 74% versus 51% retention and 3.1% versus 5.8% refund figures as evidence against the ring hypothesis.
Checks payment-instrument reuse as the deterministic first check.
Classifies clawback and account action as top rungs of the enforcement ladder, disproportionate to the evidence here.
States that proportionality overrides any efficiency ranking when choosing a rung for an individual case.
Names the word-of-mouth cost of banning the program's strongest advocate.

evals.prompt: B2B question. Northgate Analytics, we sell workspace seats, $750 account credit per referred workspace that converts to a paid annual plan. Kestrel Digital, an agency customer of ours, has referred six workspaces in eleven weeks. All six used real work email addresses on six different company domains, no free-mail addresses anywhere. Four of those domains were registered in the last 90 days. Two of the six were already running a trial with us before Kestrel's referral link was clicked. $4,500 is sitting in the payout queue. Set up the guardrails and the review process.
evals.expected_output: A B2B guardrail spec built on domain-overlap checking rather than the work-email requirement, a pipeline check applied to the two pre-trial referees, pre-payout human review, and company-account credit routing.
expectations: States that a work-email requirement alone is weak because a shell company has a real domain.
Makes domain-overlap comparison between referrer and referee the primary check, covering admin contacts, billing entity, and payment instrument.
Adds a pipeline check rejecting referrals of accounts already in the pipeline or in trial before the referral timestamp.
Applies that pipeline rule to the two referees already trialing and characterises them as routing rather than referring.
Flags the four domains registered within 90 days as an observable tell of shell-entity referral.
Makes pre-payout human review of every reward the default in B2B.
Justifies that review by per-item review cost sitting below the $750 reward value.
Routes the reward to company-account credit by default rather than to an individual employee.
Frames individual payment as a procurement or gift-policy exposure before it is a fraud problem.
Notes that in regulated sectors referral payments can be unlawful and routes that question to counsel.
States that caps, budget ceilings, hold windows, and eligibility memory work identically in B2B and B2C.

evals.prompt: Our refer-a-friend at Lumenreach - SaaS, $240/year plan, $50 referral credit - has never had a cap. Published terms say nothing about limits, eligibility, or denial. Finance has now decided on 10 rewards per referrer per year. They want it effective Monday, applied to everyone including rewards people already earned this quarter, and they want us to deny the 430 rewards currently pending under a new rule about accounts with insufficient usage that also isn't in the terms. Draft the policy.
evals.expected_output: A policy that refuses retroactive application, grandfathers the earned and pending rewards, sequences publication before enforcement, and carries a terms-status mapping marking unpublished rules as unenforceable.
expectations: States that a rule not published before a referral was made is not enforceable against that referral.
Refuses to apply the new 10-per-year cap to rewards already earned.
Recommends grandfathering the 430 pending rewards rather than denying them under the unpublished usage rule.
Sequences publication of the rules before any enforcement.
Cites the promotional-rules requirement to award advertised rewards as described and to withhold only on criteria set out beforehand.
Notes the roughly 30-day expected award timing under those promotional rules.
Notes that denying a promised reward on unstated conditions is an ordinary deception case under US doctrine.
Notes that a blanket sole-discretion clause is weaker than it is drafted to look.
Keeps the legal material as design constraints and routes the actual legal questions to counsel.
Routes the terms clause drafting to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@affiliate-program-terms.
Includes a Terms status line mapping each rule to where it is published and marking unpublished rules as not yet enforceable.

evals.prompt: Ashbrook Pet Supply. We built a referral abuse detector in-house six months ago and it auto-denies. The customer just never sees the credit appear - no email, no message, nothing on the account page. 1,100 denials last quarter and support has 340 open tickets about missing referral credit. When a case looks bad we suspend the account indefinitely pending investigation, which in practice means until someone gets to it. Our terms say we may withhold rewards at our sole discretion. Write the enforcement policy.
evals.expected_output: An enforcement policy built around published reason strings, a working appeal path with a stated SLA and human review, time-bounded investigations, and the published ladder rungs in order.
expectations: Requires a specific reason string on every reward denial.
Requires each reason string to name the published rule violated rather than an internal signal such as a device match.
Keeps internal evidence logged separately from the customer-facing reason.
Requires a working appeal path published inside the denial message itself.
States that the reason string and appeal path are built before the detection rules go live.
Sets a stated appeal response SLA and labels it self-set rather than an industry or regulatory standard.
Requires a human to review every appeal.
Rejects indefinite suspension and bounds every investigation in time.
States that the appeals-upheld rate is the program's measured false-positive rate.
Feeds the appeals-upheld rate into the friction side of the leakage/friction computation.
Instructs upholding generously on ambiguity because the friction term carries the LTV multiplier.
Lists the published ladder rungs in order: withhold pre-payout, link pause or cooldown, program removal, clawback, account action.

evals.prompt: Vendor call tomorrow. Riverbend Coffee Club, DTC subscription, card charged at signup, $40 referral credit each side, about 9,000 referrals a month. The vendor wants $4,000 a month for device fingerprinting plus their cookie-based self-referral matcher, and says those two catch most referral fraud. We already have full billing data, signup metadata, and refund records in our warehouse. What do we actually instrument, and do we buy this?
evals.expected_output: A signal plan leading with payment-instrument reuse and cohort quality, declining cookie-based linkage and treating fingerprinting as degrading, with a recommendation against the purchase.
expectations: Puts payment-instrument reuse first as the strongest deterministic signal available and already held.
Places downstream cohort quality alongside payment-instrument reuse at the top of the efficiency ordering.
Explains the tie: both already sit in billing data, neither degrades when a browser or device changes, and each catches what the other cannot.
States that cohort quality is the only signal that detects a ring of real people.
Declines to build on cookie-based linkage, citing third-party cookie blocking and the retirement of the replacement attribution APIs.
Recommends server-side attribution off billing webhooks instead of browser state.
Treats device and browser fingerprinting as degrading and overstated in strength.
Notes the fingerprinting compliance overlay, including the UK regulator position on fair choices and consent, and routes it to counsel.
Orders the remaining signals as velocity, then email similarity, then graph, then fingerprint.
Names graph or network signals as what this ordering starves, and states the condition that promotes them.
Recommends against the $4,000-a-month purchase, or defers it, in favour of signals the program already holds.

evals.prompt: Straightforward one: what are the industry-standard velocity thresholds for referral abuse? I need a number for referrals per referrer per week that counts as normal, plus the standard flag rate a healthy program should see. We're Candlewick Home, DTC candles, $20 referral credit, and we have three years of referral event history sitting in our warehouse. Board deck is Thursday.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply an industry-standard number, replaced by a derivation from Candlewick's own referrer distribution, with the background multi-accounting rate used only as a sanity anchor.
expectations: States that no referral-specific public numeric velocity threshold exists.
Refuses to supply an industry-standard velocity number presented as sourced fact.
Derives the threshold from Candlewick's own legitimate-referrer distribution, naming a p95 to p99 band of weekly referral claims.
Notes that three years of history removes any need for an illustrative placeholder threshold.
Labels any adjacent-domain convention, such as batch account-registration limits, as adjacent rather than referral-specific.
Gives the 1-2.5% multi-accounting background rate only as a sanity anchor and states its scope limitation.
States that a 20% flag rate means the rules are wrong rather than the users.
Refuses to treat any background or flag rate as a target.
Tags each threshold in the deliverable with its provenance.
Schedules a review cycle to re-derive thresholds from fresh data.
Pairs the velocity limit with a cooldown rather than an immediate ban.

evals.prompt: Mess at Sundial Skincare. Our referral code SAVE20FRIEND is now listed on three coupon aggregator sites. Referral redemptions tripled month over month but share events from actual referrers are flat, and one code converted in 14 countries we don't even ship to profitably. Our analytics lead also says a cashback browser extension is overwriting the referral attribution on a chunk of these. Marketing's proposed fix is adding a prefilled invite that mass-texts a customer's whole contact list from inside the app, so real friends outnumber strangers. Also there's no monthly ceiling on referral spend. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A response naming the leakage tells, recommending sharing restrictions plus code rotation and a budget ceiling, rejecting the mass-text invite on share-flow exposure grounds, and separating the extension issue as attribution integrity.
expectations: Identifies volume spiking without matching referrer share activity as an observable tell of code leakage.
Identifies one code converting across unrelated geographies as a second tell.
Identifies the code being indexed on public coupon pages as a third tell.
Recommends published sharing restrictions combined with code rotation.
Rejects the prefilled mass-texting invite outright.
Cites the $9M referral-program settlement as arising from the share mechanism rather than from fraud.
Names anti-spam or messaging-consent law as the exposure on the share flow.
Requires referee consent to be respected in the share flow.
States that the operator's power to cap rewards, revoke credits, and dictate sharing creates responsibility for referrer conduct.
Requires actually monitoring the published sharing rules, since retaining the ability to enforce makes non-enforcement the operator's problem.
Adds an endorsement-disclosure requirement for referred-and-rewarded customers into the sharing rules.
Separates the cashback browser extension as an attribution-integrity problem rather than a customer-enforcement one.
Sets a program-level monthly budget ceiling to bound the spend incident.

evals.prompt: We've done everything. Vireo Learning, consumer subscription, $35 referral credit each side. Over two quarters we added a 12-per-year cap, a 45-day hold, phone/SMS verification on every referred signup, and disposable-domain blocking. Abuse flags are down. But referred users still churn at 2.4x organic and refund at 3x organic, and 90-day revenue per referred account is under half of organic. Board wants another tightening pass next sprint - stricter velocity, maybe document verification. What do we tighten?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to tighten further, diagnosing the reward structure rather than the guardrails as the defect, and routing the work to the referral incentive design skill.
expectations: Recommends against a further tightening pass.
States that a referred cohort losing to organic means the program is buying signups rather than acquiring customers.
Identifies the defect as the reward structure, not the guardrails.
Routes the work to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@referral-incentive-design using that reference format.
States the scope boundary that this work protects the existing reward structure and never redesigns it.
Names a rising refund rate on the qualifying event as the signal that the event is too cheap.
Questions whether phone/SMS verification earns its friction and its messaging-consent cost at a $35 reward.
Declines to add document verification as the answer.
States that the goal is making abuse unprofitable rather than catching everything.
Recommends a referred-versus-organic cohort dashboard broken out by referrer decile as the diagnostic.
Does not claim that tighter guardrails will improve cohort quality.

evals.prompt: Launching give-15-get-15 on Thorne Budget, a personal finance app, in six weeks - it's tied to a funding announcement so the date won't move. Resourcing: one backend engineer at roughly half time, no trust-and-safety function, no fraud analyst, nobody to sit in a review queue. We want something that keeps holding as we grow, not a patch we redo every quarter. A card is required before the first paid month, so we have a payment instrument on every paying account. Write me the guardrails.
evals.expected_output: A guardrail spec that deletes manual review outright on the stated effort ceiling, promotes payment-instrument verification because the card is already collected, ships caps/hold/eligibility for the fixed date, and schedules event redesign for the next cycle.
expectations: Deletes manual review from the spec outright rather than ranking it last.
Records which controls were deleted and why, tied to the stated effort ceiling.
Moves payment-instrument verification up sharply because a card is collected before the qualifying event.
Names caps, hold, and published eligibility as the first-pass default set.
Schedules qualifying-event redesign for the next cycle rather than dropping it, because of the fixed six-week date.
Promotes eligibility memory and qualifying-event design on the stated compounding mandate.
States which stated constraint moved which control in the ordering.
States that the control ordering is a default rather than a law.
Rejects a detection-tooling-first sequencing.
Includes a cross-referrer cooldown making a referee ineligible if referred by anyone within a prior window.
Defines new customer beyond an email match, using payment instrument, delivery address, or account cluster.
States that email alone is trivially rotated.
